findings.reason: The protected Python solution iterates through the first half of string s (left in range(len(s) // 2)), compares s[left] != s[~left], counts mismatches, and early-exits returning False if mismatches > 2. Since 1 or 2 character replacements can fix up to 2 mismatched pairs (or pad an already palindromic string), the single-pass two-pointer comparison is canonical, optimal, and concise; no candidate is required.

Each mismatched pair s[left] != s[~left] requires 1 replacement to fix. If mismatches <= 2, exactly 1 or 2 operations can make s a palindrome (using center or pair modifications for 0 mismatches). If mismatches > 2, at least 3 operations are required, so returning False is correct.
Scanning at most floor(n/2) pairs takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Complexity evidence is certified and hash-bound.
Accepts lowercase English string s and returns boolean True if 1 or 2 replacements yield a palindrome, False otherwise.

The approach accurately details independent mirrored pair repairs, mismatch count thresholding <= 2, and linear O(n) time / O(1) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover string reversals, edit-distance DP overhead, already-palindromic strings, odd center characters, and early rejection at 3 mismatches.

App Python and native Python solutions both use the identical single-pass two-pointer mismatch counting algorithm with SHA-256 digests 979aa2442ae28f80b75b4757926cd0f1dd70202be323e6d5e465904d6cbc6474 and 1912237250bf5d932babbf18fd604a6084091d300ab6b09793d097a0f31b2a8b.
